strengths: Principled physical inductive bias: Formulating object interaction dynamics through low-dimensional force field prediction integrated via a second-order ODE solver effectively enforces physical consistency (governed by second-order Newton-like dynamics) and prevents arbitrary latent overfitting.

Strong few-shot and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization: The model demonstrates convincing generalization from only a few observed trajectories (e.g., 100 trajectories in I-PHYRE, 200 in N-body) to complex unseen cross-scenario configurations, significantly outperforming unconstrained latent dynamics models like SlotFormer and standard Interaction Networks.

Comprehensive evaluation and interpretability: The paper tests both within- and cross-scenario prediction as well as planning across continuous orbital mechanics and contact-rich puzzle environments. Visualizations of the learned force fields (Figures 2, 4, A2, and A3) provide clear qualitative evidence of physical interpretability.

Practical planning demonstration: Integrating the learned model into an interactive planning loop with iterative refinement demonstrates near human-level success rates on I-PHYRE, clearly outperforming both standard baselines and GPT-4o prompting.
weaknesses: Conceptual and technical novelty is somewhat incremental: The idea of parameterizing accelerations or inter-object forces via graph neural networks / DeepONet coupled with ODE numerical integrators is well-established in the literature (e.g., graph neural ODEs, neural physics engines, and related continuous-time dynamical systems). The paper needs to more clearly delineate its architectural novelty from existing physics-informed neural ODE architectures.

Handling of non-conservative and discontinuous dynamics in backward planning: In Section 3.2, backward planning via reverse time integration (Equation 6) is presented as an exact analytical inversion. However, while celestial N-body dynamics are time-reversible, contact-rich systems with friction and inelastic collisions (like I-PHYRE) are fundamentally non-conservative and irreversible. The paper only applies backward planning to N-body systems and should explicitly address the limitations and theoretical barriers to backward integration in dissipative, non-smooth contact settings.

Narrow baseline comparisons: The baselines compared against in the main experiments are limited to Interaction Networks (Battaglia et al., 2016) and SlotFormer (Wu et al., 2023). Comparing against modern physics-informed continuous-time baselines (e.g., Symplectic ODE-Net, Hamiltonian/Lagrangian networks where applicable, or modern GNN physics simulators like Sanchez-Gonzalez et al., 2020) would provide a more rigorous benchmark.

Contact dynamics and numerical stiffness: Simulating rigid collisions with standard explicit Euler integration at fixed time steps can lead to stiffness and penetration artifacts unless fine step sizes are used (as acknowledged in Section 4.5). Further discussion on how stiff contact forces and non-smooth events are handled numerically without specialized event handling would strengthen the technical soundness.

strengths: Clear motivation and physically grounded inductive bias: Parameterizing object interactions as low-dimensional force fields integrated via continuous-time ODEs provides strong regularization against overfitting in few-shot dynamics learning.

Strong empirical performance: Across both I-PHYRE and celestial N-body benchmarks, NFF demonstrates notable gains in out-of-distribution and cross-scenario prediction, substantially outperforming standard interaction networks and slot-based baselines.

Interpretability and analytical utility: Explicit force field modeling allows meaningful visualization of underlying physical effects (e.g., normal force, spring displacement, gravity) and enables bidirectional simulation for initial condition discovery in planning tasks.

Comprehensive experimental analysis: The paper includes extensive ablation studies on integration order, solver step sizes, latent dimensionality, and interactive refinement rounds, along with detailed qualitative visualizations in the appendix.
weaknesses: Incremental technical novelty: Combining graph-based pairwise interaction networks with second-order numerical integration (Newtonian acceleration/force prediction integrated into velocity and position) is well-explored in physics-informed machine learning and neural dynamical systems. The distinction from existing continuous-time graph physics engines should be articulated more clearly.

Handling of non-smooth dynamics: Rigid-body contacts, impulse collisions, and abrupt eliminations in I-PHYRE represent non-smooth dynamical systems. Standard continuous ODE integrators (e.g., fixed-step Euler) generally struggle with stiff contact constraints and penetration; the paper could provide more formal discussion or empirical analysis regarding how NFF handles stiff impact singularities.

Fairness and clarity of baseline setup: SlotFormer is primarily designed for unsupervised object discovery from raw visual input, whereas NFF operates on privileged symbolic state vectors (positions, velocities, spring indices). The exact adaptation of SlotFormer to symbolic states warrants more explicit detail to ensure an apples-to-apples comparison.

Formatting and presentation artifacts: The running header on pages 2 through 20 displays 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size', indicating a lack of proofreading with the LaTeX conference template.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and ambitious problem: achieving sample-efficient, out-of-distribution generalization and planning in physical reasoning tasks.

Evaluating the learned representations across both forward simulation and planning tasks (using I-PHYRE and N-body dynamics) provides a diverse testbed of rigid-body contact mechanics and gravitational interactions.
The ablation studies examine relevant practical aspects such as integration step size, representation dimensionality, and numerical solver choice.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual and methodological novelty: The core architecture models pairwise interactions on a graph and outputs accelerations integrated via standard numerical ODE solvers (such as Euler). This framework is conceptually almost identical to standard Graph Neural Network-based physics simulators (e.g., Interaction Networks, Sanchez-Gonzalez et al.) and continuous-time neural ODE formulations. Framing this as a novel foundational framework ('Neural Force Field') overstates the technical contribution.

Unsound formulation of backward planning: Section 3.2 and Equation (6) claim that initial conditions can be analytically computed given a desired goal state by integrating backwards. However, for dissipative and non-conservative dynamical systems involving contact, friction, and collision (such as I-PHYRE), dynamics are strictly non-invertible. Furthermore, backwards integration requires knowledge of the state trajectory $z(t)$ over the entire interval $[0, t]$, which is unavailable when only the final goal state is specified. The paper does not adequately explain how this fundamental ill-posedness is resolved.

Weak and narrow baseline selection: The method is only compared against Interaction Networks (from 2016) and SlotFormer. SlotFormer was originally proposed for visual, unsupervised slot-based dynamics rather than symbolic state trajectory modeling. Modern physical reasoning and continuous-time dynamics baselines (e.g., Hamiltonian/Lagrangian Neural Networks, Symplectic ODE-Nets, or modern Graph Network Simulators) are omitted.

Oversimplified experimental assumptions: In I-PHYRE, all object masses are assumed to be identical, and the mass term is absorbed directly into the learned force field. This severely limits the claim of learning true Newtonian physical principles, as the model does not decouple mass and force, limiting its transferability to scenarios with heterogeneous mass distributions.

Drafting and presentation issues: The running header across pages 2–11 displays the uncompiled template placeholder 'Title Suppressed Due to Excessive Size', indicating a lack of polish before submission.

strengths: Sound physics-informed inductive bias: Formulating object interaction via continuous force fields parameterized by neural operators and integrating trajectories with explicit numerical ODE solvers provides strong structural priors for physical reasoning.

Remarkable sample efficiency and OOD generalization: Demonstrates convincing few-shot learning capabilities across multiple benchmarks (I-PHYRE, N-body, and PHYRE), outperforming baselines like Interaction Networks and SlotFormer, particularly in cross-scenario and extended-horizon prediction.

Comprehensive task evaluation: Evaluates both state-based and vision-based domains across forward trajectory prediction, interactive goal-directed planning, and initial condition reconstruction via backward time integration.
Thorough ablation and empirical analysis: The paper provides informative ablations covering integration order/step-size, ODE grounding, operator formulation (DeepONet vs. MLP), and noise robustness.
weaknesses: Incremental algorithmic novelty: Integrating neural network-predicted accelerations or forces via ODE solvers over graph representations is well-established in the graph dynamical systems literature (e.g., Graph ODEs, Hamiltonian/Lagrangian Neural Networks, and physics-informed GNN simulators). The primary novelty lies in combining DeepONet with ODE integration for few-shot physical reasoning benchmarks rather than introducing a fundamentally new theoretical mechanism.

Handling of non-smooth collision dynamics: Rigid-body contacts and collisions involve discontinuous velocity jumps (impulses) and high stiffness. Modeling these interactions purely as smooth continuous force fields with standard Euler/Runge-Kutta integrators can lead to interpenetration or numerical instability in higher-velocity or higher-friction regimes.

Clarity and fairness in visual PHYRE setup: The vision-based PHYRE setup relies on object segmentation masks and sparse convolutions to predict translations and rotations. It is not entirely clear whether all compared baselines have access to identical object-level mask supervision and geometric decomposition, which could account for some of the performance gap over end-to-end pixel models.

Evaluation limited to stylized 2D/point-mass benchmarks: While the three tested benchmarks are diverse, they are restricted to 2D toy environments and celestial point masses. Demonstrating scalability to complex 3D contact dynamics (e.g., in MuJoCo, Physion, or real-world robotic manipulation) would significantly substantiate the broader physical world model claims.

strengths: Well-motivated physical inductive bias: Formulating object interactions as continuous neural operator force fields integrated via an ODE solver enforces Newtonian consistency, effectively preventing common failure modes of latent transition models such as object disappearance and shape morphing.

Strong sample efficiency and out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization: The model achieves superior cross-scenario prediction and planning across I-PHYRE, N-body, and PHYRE while using orders of magnitude less training data than existing state-of-the-art baselines.

Efficient backward planning: Formulating transitions via an explicit continuous dynamical system enables fast and exact backward integration for goal-directed initial condition estimation (as demonstrated in N-body tasks), avoiding costly iterative optimization.

Thorough evaluation: The paper conducts comprehensive evaluations covering forward prediction, multi-round interactive planning with refinement, robustness to noisy perceptions, and detailed ablations on numerical integration methods, step sizes, and operator architectures.
weaknesses: Handling of non-smooth contact and collision dynamics: Explicit ODE solvers (such as Euler with fixed step size) typically struggle with stiff differential equations and discontinuity events inherent to rigid-body collisions, which can lead to interpenetration or energy drift unless very small step sizes are used.

Reliance on visual masks for vision-based tasks: On PHYRE, the approach relies on masked sparse convolutions, assuming access to instance segmentation masks across time, which restricts its direct application to unstructured, raw video without pre-existing object detectors.

Coupled mass and material assumptions: As acknowledged in the limitations, the framework absorbs mass, friction, and restitution into the learned force field based on visible geometric properties (e.g., size), which limits generalization to objects with identical geometry but drastically differing densities or surface properties.

strengths: Principled physics-grounded inductive bias: Modeling dynamics by explicitly predicting low-dimensional continuous force fields via a neural operator on interaction graphs, followed by second-order ODE numerical integration, provides strong physical consistency compared to purely discrete latent transition models.

Strong few-shot and out-of-distribution generalization: The empirical evaluation across three benchmarks (I-PHYRE, 3D N-body, and PHYRE) demonstrates significant sample efficiency and superior cross-scenario generalization compared to baselines like IN, GCN, and SlotFormer.

Bi-directional simulation utility: The continuous and invertible ODE formulation enables not only forward trajectory rollout for forward planning, but also reverse-time integration for rapid backward optimization of initial conditions (as shown in the N-body planning experiments).

Comprehensive empirical analysis: The submission provides thorough ablation studies (evaluating integration precision, ODE grounding vs. discrete transition, and DeepONet vs. MLP), noise robustness tests, and qualitative force-field visualizations.
weaknesses: Handling of non-smooth contact and collision dynamics: Classical ODE integrators assume smooth vector fields, whereas rigid body collisions typically involve instantaneous velocity jumps, impulses, and non-penetration constraints. The paper does not formally address how stiff contact discontinuities are resolved beyond small-step numerical integration.

Conflation of force and acceleration: The paper notes that mass constants are absorbed into the learned force field F(z). In Newtonian mechanics, F/m = a; if mass is not explicitly factored or decoupled, the network learns an acceleration field rather than a true transferable force field, which may limit generalization across varying masses and densities.

Input representation parity across baselines on PHYRE: On the PHYRE benchmark, NFF relies on sparse convolutions over explicit object segmentation masks. It is unclear whether all baseline architectures (e.g., RPIN, SlotFormer) were provided with identical segmented representations and state features, making it hard to decouple the benefits of the force-field ODE formulation from the perceptual representation.

Incremental technical novelty over existing physics-informed neural ODEs: The combination of graph neural networks/neural operators with ODE solvers (e.g., Hamiltonian/Lagrangian neural networks, EGODE, 2nd-order Neural ODEs) is well-studied in dynamical systems; the core novelty lies primarily in its application to few-shot physical reasoning puzzles.
